title: Magazine review of his banjo and his mandolin-like sound
summary: Rolf reads a review praising Guesnon over Marrero; Guesnon explains his wrist technique that makes the banjo sound like a mandolin.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: he say, I'd go to Duke Ellington's band. I like this. From the Eureka magazine. A much more satisfactory four-four beat, as is the playing of, in the LP under Robinson's name. Geno is much better than Marrero. His rhythm playing is lighter and harder for him. Yeah, I think what I'm sure. And he plays jazz solos, well constructed and melodic.

That's quite true. Well, I mean, well the Cressnos, like I say, you seek for more, you find more. I mean, Lawrence, I mean, I tried to break him with that. It became too much of a monotonous thing. Everything was too, heavy. And it just never, the change never stroked. You know what I mean? The stroke never changed. I mean, it was, you see, but you don't have to play like that. Instead of trying, you judge from your wrist. Uh-huh. Of what you must do. When they become loud, when they get soft. Yeah. That's right. I mean, you see. Now the other fella that wrote a little thing, said that I had a knack of making a banjo sound like a mandolin. And that's true. You listen to that solo on Savoy Blues, on that blue note. That don't sound like no banjo. It sound like a melodic mandolin. Yeah, sure. You listen at it. Yeah, yeah, yeah. A mandolin effect. Yeah.

That's done with the wrist, you see. While I'm, you see, while I'm picking, I'm easing up on the vibration on the wrist. I mean, that's right. Do you think you ever have, have you ever been better than just that time?
